Here are several proven strategies an apartment building can adopt to reduce its heating costs. Many of these measures will also improve comfort and may raise your EPC energy class (epc_egienergiklass) when re‐assessed:

1. Review Your Current Energy Performance  
   • Obtain or update your Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) to confirm your current energy class (epc_egienergiklass). If there are multiple certificates, always refer to the most recent one.  
   • The EPC will highlight your building’s biggest heat losses (e.g. walls, roof, windows) and suggest cost-effective improvements.

2. Improve the Building Envelope  
   • Insulation  
     – Loft/attic: Add or top up insulation to at least 300 mm if it’s below recommended levels.  
     – External walls: Consider external or internal wall insulation, especially on solid-walled façades.  
     – Basement and ground floor: Insulate under suspended timber floors or install slab insulation under concrete floors.  
   • Windows and Doors  
     – Upgrade to high-performance double- or triple-glazed units with low-emissivity (low-E) coatings and thermally broken frames.  
     – Seal gaps with weatherstripping to reduce draughts around sashes, frames and entry doors.

3. Optimize the Heating System  
   • Upgrade Boilers and Heat Generators  
     – Replace old boilers with high-efficiency condensing boilers or consider a small heat pump (air-to-water or ground-source) for central heating.  
   • Controls and Zoning  
     – Install programmable thermostats or smart thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) to control temperatures by time of day and by zone (e.g. corridors, apartments).  
     – Add room sensors and a building management system (BMS) for larger properties to monitor and adjust heat based on actual demand.  
   • Distribution and Maintenance  
     – Balance the radiators so each dwelling or zone receives the required flow and avoid “over-heating” close to the boiler.  
     – Flush and clean the central heating system regularly to remove sludge and improve flow efficiency.

4. Recover and Reuse Waste Heat  
   • Mechanical Ventilation with Heat Recovery (MVHR)  
     – In buildings with controlled ventilation, MVHR units recover up to 90% of the outgoing air’s heat to pre-heat incoming fresh air.  
   • Heat Pumps on Wastewater  
     – For larger developments, systems can extract heat from wastewater (e.g. showers) to feed back into pre-heating domestic hot water.

5. Shift to Renewable or Lower-Cost Energy Sources  
   • District Heating  
     – Where available, district heating networks often supply heat more cheaply and at higher efficiency than individual boilers.  
   • Solar Thermal and Photovoltaics  
     – Solar thermal panels can pre-heat domestic hot water.  
     – PV panels paired with electric heat pumps can offset electricity use and provide low-carbon heating.

6. Smart Operation and Occupant Engagement  
   • Automated Scheduling  
     – Use time-of-use tariffs and schedule heating to run at lower power during off-peak hours or when residents are away.  
   • Tenant Information  
     – Provide guidance on setting thermostats (e.g. 20–21 °C in living spaces, lower in corridors), airing rooms without leaving windows wide open, and using radiator foil behind panels on external walls.

7. Financial Incentives and Phased Implementation  
   • Government Grants and Rebates  
     – Investigate local or national subsidies designed to upgrade EPC classes, install heat pumps or improve insulation.  
   • Phased Retrofit  
     – Tackle the most cost-effective measures first (usually loft and cavity wall insulation), then plan more capital-intensive upgrades (boiler replacement, MVHR) in subsequent phases.

By following a structured approach—starting with your EPC (epc_egienergiklass), targeting the highest heat-loss areas, and combining envelope improvements with modern heating controls—you can typically reduce heating costs by 20–50%, improve resident comfort and move your building into a higher energy performance class.

An energy declaration (Energideklaration) gives a building board a clear, standardized overview of the property’s current energy performance and points the way toward cost-effective efficiency improvements.  Typically it includes:

• Energy performance rating  
  – A letter grade (A–G) and a numeric indicator (kWh/m²·year), showing how the building compares to national benchmarks.  
  – If multiple assessments exist, the most recent class is the valid one.  

• Actual or calculated energy use  
  – Breakdown by heating, hot water, ventilation, lighting, etc.  
  – Total heated floor area (Atemp), number of above-ground floors and stairwells—all helping to normalize consumption figures.  

• Building characteristics  
  – Construction type (e.g. detached house, apartment block) and age or period of construction.  
  – Primary heating system and fuel type, insulation levels in walls, roof and windows.  

• Recommended measures  
  – Insulation upgrades, window replacement, ventilation improvements, heating-system optimizations or control-system installations.  
  – Estimated energy savings, investment costs and payback times for each measure.  

• Compliance and documentation  
  – Confirms that the building meets current regulatory requirements.  
  – Provides a basis for long-term energy planning, budget forecasting and potential subsidy or loan applications.  

By reviewing an energy declaration, a building board can prioritize retrofit projects, track improvements over time and demonstrate to residents or stakeholders that energy-efficiency is being systematically managed.

To reduce your building’s heating costs, you should focus on measures that improve the thermal performance of the building envelope and optimize your heating system. Even without specific EPC data, the following priorities generally deliver the biggest savings:

1. Enhance Insulation  
   • Roof/Ceiling – Upgrading loft or attic insulation typically yields the highest return, as heat rises and is lost through the top of the building.  
   • External Walls – Adding or improving wall insulation (either internally or externally) cuts significant heat losses through masonry or timber walls.  
   • Ground/Floor Slabs – Insulating suspended timber floors or solid ground slabs reduces cold‐bridging and drafts at ground level.

2. Improve Airtightness  
   • Seal Gaps – Identify and seal cracks around windows, doors, penetrations for pipes/cables, and junctions between building elements to prevent draughts.  
   • Controlled Ventilation – Pair airtightness work with a mechanical ventilation system that has a heat-recovery unit (MVHR) to maintain indoor air quality without losing heat.

3. Upgrade Windows and Doors  
   • Double- or Triple-Glazing – Modern glazing units with low-emissivity coatings and insulated frames will reduce both conductive and radiative heat loss.  
   • Weather-Stripping – Renew seals on existing frames to stop cold air ingress.

4. Optimize Heating System  
   • High-Efficiency Boiler or Heat Pump – Replace old boilers (especially ones older than 15 years) with A-rated condensing boilers or air-/ground-source heat pumps.  
   • Smart Controls – Install programmable thermostats and thermostatic radiator valves to tailor heating schedules and temperature zones to actual occupancy.  
   • System Balancing – Ensure radiators and under-floor circuits are properly balanced so that the system operates evenly and avoids overheating.

5. Operational Measures and Monitoring  
   • Regular Maintenance – Service boilers, inspect pipe insulation and bleed radiators to keep the system running at peak efficiency.  
   • Energy Monitoring – Install simple meters or building-management software to track consumption patterns and identify waste.  
   • Occupant Engagement – Encourage temperate thermostat settings (e.g. 19–21 °C) and small behavioral changes, like closing doors to unused rooms.

6. Long-Term Upgrades  
   • Solar Gain and Shading – Where appropriate, use south-facing glazing or solar collectors; add external shading to avoid overheating in summer.  
   • Renewable Integration – Consider photovoltaic panels or solar thermal systems to offset electricity or hot-water costs.

By systematically targeting the building envelope first (insulation and airtightness) and then optimizing the heating plant and controls, you can typically achieve 20–40 % reductions in heating energy use—and corresponding cost savings—without compromising comfort.

Direct-acting electric radiators (sometimes called direct-acting convectors or panel heaters) convert virtually 100 percent of the electricity they draw into heat at the point of use. In that narrow sense they’re “efficient” – there is no combustion loss and no heat distribution loss through pipework or ducting.  

However, when evaluating overall energy efficiency and cost, two things are important:  

1. Primary energy and generation losses  
   • Electricity production (especially from fossil fuels or nuclear) typically incurs conversion losses in power plants (only roughly 35–50 percent of the primary fuel energy becomes grid-delivered electricity).  
   • Grid transmission and distribution also incur losses (5–10 percent on average).  
   Consequently, each kWh of electricity you pay for may represent 2–3 kWh (or more) of primary energy.  

2. Alternative heating systems’ efficiency  
   • Air- or ground-source heat pumps can achieve coefficients of performance (COP) of 3–5, meaning they deliver 3–5 kWh of heat per kWh of electricity.  
   • District heating, biomass boilers or highly efficient condensing gas boilers may likewise deliver heat more cost-effectively (in terms of primary energy and climate impact).  

Practical considerations  
• Control and zoning: Modern direct‐acting electric radiators with built-in thermostats, timers and “open‐window” detection can limit wasted energy by heating only when and where needed.  
• Installation cost: Electric radiators are inexpensive and quick to install – attractive for retrofits, secondary spaces (garages, attics, seldom-used rooms) or where extending a water-based system is impractical.  
• Running cost: Because electricity typically costs more per kWh than district heat or gas, running direct electric radiators as your sole heat source tends to be more expensive.  

Summary  
• Point-of-use efficiency: ~100 percent.  
• Whole-system (primary energy) efficiency: relatively low, due to generation and grid losses.  
• Competitiveness: outclassed by heat pumps, district heating or high-efficiency boilers for continuous whole-house heating.  
• Best use cases: spot-heating, supplementing an existing system, or in very well-insulated buildings with intermittent or low-level heating needs.

Here are several practical ways to get the best performance and lowest running cost from direct-acting electric radiators:

1. Thermostat control and scheduling  
   • Fit each radiator with its own programmable or smart thermostat.  
   • Set lower “ setback” temperatures (e.g. 15–17 °C) when you’re asleep or out, and raise to comfort level (20–21 °C) only when needed.  
   • Use weekly or daily schedules so radiators come on shortly before you wake up or return home, rather than heating continuously.

2. Zoning and room-by-room adjustment  
   • Divide your home into heating zones (living areas, bedrooms, guest rooms) and treat each independently.  
   • Close doors to unused rooms and turn those radiators completely off or to frost-protection mode (around 5 °C).  
   • Balance individual radiator settings so you don’t overheat some rooms while others stay cold.

3. Take advantage of off-peak tariffs  
   • If your electricity supplier offers a two-tariff (day-night) meter, program heaters to draw more power during the cheaper night-rate period.  
   • Combine with storage or fan-assisted models that can absorb heat overnight and release it slowly by day.

4. Improve building fabric and radiator efficiency  
   • Insulate walls, lofts and floors to reduce overall heat loss—this lets your radiators maintain comfort with less output.  
   • Fit low-emissivity reflective foil behind radiators on external walls to push more heat into the room rather than into the wall.  
   • Keep radiators unobstructed—avoid placing furniture, curtains or clothes immediately in front of them.

5. Maintenance and good practice  
   • Dust and vacuum radiators and fans regularly so heat transfer isn’t impeded.  
   • Check thermostatic valves and sensors for proper operation—replace faulty units promptly.  
   • Take care when redecorating or moving furniture to avoid damaging electrical connections.

6. Advanced controls (optional)  
   • Consider linking radiators to a home-automation system or smart-home hub for voice control, geofencing (heating on when you arrive) and energy-use monitoring.  
   • Use adaptive learning thermostats that track your schedule and outdoor temperature, then fine-tune switching patterns for maximum efficiency.

By combining good insulation, individual room control, scheduled setbacks and regular maintenance, you’ll keep occupants comfortable while minimizing the electricity cost of direct-acting radiators.

Improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot-water systems typically involves reducing heat losses, raising system performance and, where possible, making use of renewable or waste-heat sources. Key measures include:

1. Better insulation  
   • Insulate the storage cylinder (tank) with a high-performance jacket or foam wrap to reduce standby losses.  
   • Insulate all hot-water distribution pipes and fittings (valves, elbows, etc.) to minimize losses in the network.  

2. Temperature control and set-points  
   • Lower the storage temperature to the minimum safe level (usually around 55–60 °C) and install a thermostatic mixing valve at outlets to prevent scalding.  
   • Use a programmable controller or smart thermostat to reduce tank temperature further during periods of low or no demand (e.g. overnight or when occupants are away).  

3. Upgrade to high-efficiency heat sources  
   • Replace old electric or combustion water heaters with heat-pump water heaters, which can achieve 2–4× the efficiency of electric resistance models.  
   • If you already have a boiler or heat pump for space heating, install an integrated or cascade water-heating module to share the same low-temperature heat source.  

4. Solar thermal and renewable integration  
   • Add solar-thermal collectors on the roof or façade to preheat incoming cold water, reducing the load on the backup heater.  
   • Combine photovoltaics with a heat-pump water heater (PV-driven HPWH) to make use of self-generated electricity.  

5. Waste-heat recovery  
   • Install a drain-water heat-recovery unit under showers to capture and transfer heat from warm wastewater into the incoming cold feed.  
   • In buildings with mechanical ventilation and heat recovery (MVHR), consider coupling the ventilation-air heat exchanger to domestic hot water preheating.  

6. Demand-control strategies  
   • Use point-of-use (tankless) electric or gas water heaters close to high-use fixtures (kitchens, bathrooms) to eliminate distribution losses in long pipe runs.  
   • Implement occupancy or flow sensors to run recirculation pumps only when there is likely to be demand, rather than continuously.  

7. Regular maintenance and monitoring  
   • Flush the cylinder periodically to remove sediment, which impairs heat transfer.  
   • Check and service controls, valves and burners (for combustion heaters) to ensure optimum performance.  
   • Fit temperature and flow meters or a simple energy monitor to track consumption and verify that efficiency upgrades are delivering expected savings.  

By combining good insulation, precise controls, efficient heat sources and—where feasible—renewable or waste-heat inputs, it is possible to cut domestic hot-water energy use by 30–60 percent compared with a typical uninsulated electric-resistance or older gas-fired system.

Optimizing domestic hot-water production in an apartment building involves a combination of technical upgrades, system design improvements and operational measures. Below are several strategies you can consider:

1. Centralized Heat Pump System  
   • Install a high-efficiency water-to-water heat pump sized to match the building’s hot-water demand profile.  
   • Recover heat from other building sources (e.g. ventilations exhaust air, condenser water from cooling systems) to pre-heat domestic hot water.  

2. Solar Thermal Integration  
   • Mount solar-thermal collectors on the roof to pre-heat storage tanks during sunny months.  
   • Pair solar pre-heat with a backup boiler or heat pump to ensure year-round reliability.  

3. Storage-Tank Optimization  
   • Use well-insulated, stratified hot-water storage tanks to minimize standby losses and maintain thermal layers.  
   • Size buffer volumes appropriately to avoid short-cycling of heat sources and ensure rapid response to peak loads.  

4. Distribution System Improvements  
   • Insulate all hot-water pipes and circulations loops to reduce distribution losses.  
   • Implement a demand-controlled circulation pump that runs only when there is a call for hot water or scheduled peak-use times.  

5. Advanced Controls & Metering  
   • Install temperature sensors and programmable controllers to maintain supply water at the minimum permissible temperature (e.g. 55 °C) to limit heat losses yet prevent legionella.  
   • Use individual apartment sub-meters for hot-water consumption to encourage tenant conservation and enable cost-recovery billing.  

6. Waste-Water Heat Recovery  
   • Fit heat-recovery units on shower drains or grey-water outlets. These units transfer energy from warm wastewater to preheat incoming fresh water.  

7. Regular Maintenance & Commissioning  
   • Flush and clean heat-exchanger surfaces periodically to preserve efficiency.  
   • Verify setpoints, pump schedules and insulation integrity at least annually.  

8. Tenant Engagement and Education  
   • Provide guidance on using thermostatic mixer valves, efficient showerheads and flow‐reducing aerators.  
   • Share consumption data and best practices to encourage behavior that reduces unnecessary hot-water use.  

By combining these measures—selecting efficient heat sources, minimizing losses in storage and distribution, and engaging residents in efficient use—you can significantly reduce energy consumption and operating costs while maintaining comfort and safety in the building.

An energy declaration (in Swedish, “energideklaration”) is an official document that describes and rates a building’s energy performance. It is prepared by a certified energy expert and contains the following key elements:  
• Building identification and basic characteristics (type of building, heated floor area, number of floors, stairwells, etc.)  
• Calculated annual energy use (typically expressed in kWh/m² per year)  
• An energy class rating—labelled A through G—where A indicates the most energy‐efficient buildings and G the least (if multiple certificates exist, the most recent rating is the valid one)  
• Recommendations for cost‐effective measures to improve energy efficiency (for example, upgrading insulation, replacing windows or optimizing heating systems)  

In Sweden, an energy declaration is mandatory when certain buildings are constructed, sold or offered for rent. Its purpose is to give property owners, buyers and tenants clear, comparable information about expected energy costs and to highlight opportunities for reducing consumption and environmental impact.

Energy-efficiency improvement in the context of a building means any upgrade, retrofit or operational change that lowers the amount of energy required to maintain comfortable and healthy indoor conditions—primarily heating, cooling, ventilation, lighting and domestic hot water.  By improving energy efficiency you reduce energy bills, cut greenhouse-gas emissions and often enhance occupant comfort.

Typical measures include:
• Building envelope upgrades  
  – Adding or upgrading insulation in walls, roofs and floors  
  – Replacing single- or poorly sealed windows with high-performance glazing  
  – Sealing air leaks around doors, windows and service penetrations  
• Heating, cooling and ventilation system upgrades  
  – Installing a high-efficiency boiler, heat pump or district-heating connection  
  – Adding heat-recovery ventilation to recover waste heat from exhaust air  
  – Zoning controls or smart thermostats for more precise temperature management  
• Lighting and domestic appliances  
  – Converting to LED or other high-efficacy lamps  
  – Specifying energy-efficient pumps, motors and household appliances  
• Building management and controls  
  – Automated energy-management systems that optimize plant operation  
  – Occupancy and daylight sensors to reduce unnecessary lighting and cooling  

On an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC), these improvements will raise the building’s energy class (epc_egienergiklass) and lower its calculated energy use per square metre (epc_egenatemp contributes to that calculation as the heated floor area). The EPC will usually list recommended measures in order of cost-effectiveness. Implementing them one or more at a time—starting with the most impactful—constitutes an energy-efficiency improvement programme.

In general, a “premise” (lokal) in a property is any distinct functional space that has its own use, occupants and often its own energy profile. Common types include:

1. Residential units  
   – Detached houses, semi-detached or row houses, apartments, student or senior housing.  
   – Energy drivers: space heating dominated by envelope losses (walls, roof, windows), domestic hot water, lighting and appliances. Typical occupancy peaks in mornings and evenings.  

2. Office and administrative premises  
   – Open-plan offices, cell offices, meeting rooms, reception areas.  
   – Energy drivers: high lighting loads, office equipment (computers, servers), moderate heating and cooling (set‐point ~20–22 °C), continuous ventilation during office hours.  

3. Retail and service premises  
   – Shops, restaurants, cafés, hairdressers, showrooms.  
   – Energy drivers: lighting (often accent/spot lighting), refrigeration (in food stores or restaurants), ventilation (especially kitchens), variable occupancy patterns including evenings and weekends.  

4. Industrial and workshop premises  
   – Factories, assembly halls, workshops, labs.  
   – Energy drivers: process heat or cooling, heavy machinery, compressed air, large open volumes (high heat losses), sometimes very high power demand for specific processes.  

5. Storage and warehousing  
   – Cold stores, general warehousing, archive rooms.  
   – Energy drivers: refrigeration in cold stores, lower heating set-points in non-climate-controlled warehouses, large roof and wall areas leading to significant transmission losses.  

6. Garages and parking facilities  
   – Enclosed or semi-open car parks, bike storage.  
   – Energy drivers: lighting, sometimes ventilation (CO₂ removal), generally lower heating demand if not fully climate-controlled.  

7. Common and technical areas  
   – Corridors, stairwells, lobbies, basements, plant and equipment rooms.  
   – Energy drivers: continuous or timed lighting, some heating or frost protection, plus the energy for building services (pumps, lifts, fans).  

How premises type affects total energy consumption  
• Internal loads and usage hours differ greatly. Offices and retail spaces have high equipment and lighting loads during business hours, whereas residential uses spike mornings and evenings.  
• Temperature set-points vary: habitable rooms are typically kept at 20–22 °C, storage or garage spaces often lower.  
• Ventilation requirements drive heating and cooling loads—restaurants and industrial halls often need high air change rates.  
• Process energy (manufacturing, refrigeration) can dominate in industrial or food-service premises.  
• Building geometry (number of floors, stairwells, heated floor area/Atemp) influences transmission losses: more exterior surface per square meter of floor area means higher heating demand.  

By identifying and separating each premise type, energy assessments (e.g., in an EPC) can be tailored to the actual use patterns, internal loads and envelope characteristics, leading to more accurate consumption estimates and targeted efficiency measures.

In multi-unit or multi-story buildings, electricity in shared spaces such as corridors, lobbies and lift shafts is almost entirely consumed by building services and safety systems.  The main uses are:

1. Lighting  
   • General lighting in corridors, stairwells and lobbies (often on time-clock or presence sensors)  
   • Emergency/escape-route lighting (on separate circuits with battery or central UPS back-up)  

2. Vertical transport (lifts & escalators)  
   • Drive motors and control electronics for passenger and service elevators  
   • Hall call/button panels and lobby display indicators  
   • Standby lighting inside lift cars (often on a small emergency battery)  

3. Ventilation, smoke-extraction and air-handling  
   • Extract and supply fans serving corridors or lobbies  
   • Smoke-extraction fans in stairwells or lift lobbies (fire-safe systems)  

4. Fire and life-safety systems  
   • Fire-alarm panels, detectors and sounders in common areas  
   • Door-release mechanisms on fire doors or magnetic hold-open devices  

5. Access control and security  
   • Electronic door-entry systems (intercoms, card readers) at lobby entrances  
   • CCTV cameras and recording equipment covering corridors or lifts  

6. Convenience outlets and small services  
   • Cleaning-equipment sockets in service cupboards or on each floor  
   • Sign-parking displays, directory boards or digital notice-screens  

Depending on the building’s design and the local energy-management strategy, these loads may be met through time-of-use tariffs, on-site generation (e.g. solar panels) or controlled via a building-automation system to minimise peak consumption.

Apartment buildings often offer significant opportunities for reducing energy use and peak demand. The most common efficiency measures fall into four main categories: building envelope, heating/ventilation, lighting and controls, and on-site renewable generation. Below is a concise overview of each.  
  
1. Building Envelope  
• Wall insulation upgrades – adding or improving insulation in cavity walls or exterior façades to reduce heat loss.  
• Roof and ceiling insulation – installing or topping up insulation in attics or flat roofs.  
• Floor insulation – applying insulation under ground-floor slabs or in suspended timber floors.  
• High-performance windows and doors – replacing single-glazed units with double- or triple-glazed, low-U-value frames; improving air tightness around openings.  
  
2. Heating, Ventilation and Domestic Hot Water (DHW)  
• Heat-recovery ventilation (HRV) – balanced mechanical ventilation systems that recover heat from exhaust air.  
• Condensing boilers – higher-efficiency gas or oil boilers that capture latent heat from flue gases.  
• Heat pumps – air-source or ground-source heat pumps for space heating and/or DHW.  
• District heating connections – tapping into local district energy networks where available.  
• Pipework insulation – wrapping distribution pipes and tanks to minimize thermal losses.  
  
3. Lighting, Appliances and Controls  
• LED lighting retrofits – replacing fluorescent or incandescent fittings with LEDs, often combined with occupancy and daylight sensors.  
• Smart metering and building-energy management systems – real-time monitoring and automated control of heating, cooling and lighting based on occupancy and time schedules.  
• High-efficiency domestic appliances – encouraging tenants to choose A-rated refrigerators, washing machines, etc., or installing central shared laundry with efficient equipment.  
  
4. On-site Renewable Energy and Storage  
• Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels – roof-mounted or façade-integrated PV to generate electricity for common areas or tenant use.  
• Solar thermal collectors – pre-heating domestic hot water to reduce boiler or heat-pump load.  
• Battery storage – capturing excess PV output for use during peak periods or after dark.  
  
Additional measures can include:  
• Smart thermostatic radiator valves or zone controls to tailor heating in individual apartments rather than heating the entire building uniformly.  
• Building-wide commissioning and routine maintenance to ensure systems operate as designed over time.  
• Tenant engagement and behaviour programs to promote energy-conscious use of heating, hot water and lighting.  
  
When combined, these measures can typically reduce apartment-building energy consumption by 30–60%, lower operating costs for owners and tenants, and contribute to greenhouse-gas emission targets.

In most residential and commercial properties, electricity consumption breaks down into a handful of major end-uses. Although the exact share of each category varies with climate, building design and occupant behavior, the following uses are typically the largest:

1. Space Heating and Cooling  
   – In colder climates where electric heating is used (e.g. heat pumps, electric radiators), space heating can account for 30–50 % of total electricity.  
   – In warmer climates or well-insulated buildings with air-conditioning, cooling (air-conditioning compressors, fan coils) may likewise represent a similar share.

2. Domestic Hot Water  
   – Electric water heaters (storage tanks or instant/flow-through units) generally consume 15–25 % of a home’s electricity.

3. Lighting  
   – Residential lighting runs between 5 % and 15 % of total use (higher in older buildings using incandescent/halogen lamps, lower in buildings with LEDs).  
   – In commercial or industrial properties, lighting can be up to 25 % or more of the electricity load, especially where high-bay or exterior lighting is in constant use.

4. Household Appliances and Plug Loads  
   – Refrigerators, freezers, cooking stoves, laundry machines, dishwashers and kitchen auxiliaries typically consume 15–20 % of a home’s electricity.  
   – “Plug loads” — TVs, computers, chargers, entertainment systems, medical equipment — can add another 10–15 %.

5. Ventilation, Pumps and Fans  
   – Mechanical ventilation fans, heat-recovery units, circulation pumps for hydronic systems and boiler feed pumps consume roughly 5–10 % of total electricity.  
   – In larger buildings (hotels, offices, hospitals), central air-handling units and distribution fans can drive this share higher.

6. Elevators, Escalators and Specialized Equipment  
   – In multi-story residential or commercial buildings, lifts and escalators may represent 2–5 %.  
   – Any specialized equipment (kitchen hoods, laundry dryers, laboratory or medical devices) will add to this baseline.

Summary of Typical Shares (Residential Example)  
• Space heating (electric): 30–50 %  
• Hot water: 15–25 %  
• Appliances & plug loads: 25–35 %  
• Lighting: 5–15 %  
• Ventilation/pumps: 5–10 %  
• Miscellaneous (elevators, specialty equipment): 2–5 %

Keep in mind that improving the efficiency of major end-uses (for example by installing a high-COP heat pump, switching to LED lighting, or choosing Energy Star appliances) will have the greatest impact on reducing overall electricity use.

Natural (or passive) ventilation uses natural forces—wind pressure and the stack (buoyancy) effect—to move fresh air through a building, rather than relying on fans and ductwork.  Compared to mechanical ventilation systems, its main advantages are:

1. Energy savings  
   • No fans or blowers means very low operational electricity demand.  
   • Reduces heating/cooling loads when used in mild climates or at night (night‐time cooling).

2. Lower capital and maintenance costs  
   • Simpler equipment (vents, windows, vents with automatic controls) is cheaper to install than a full fan-and-duct system.  
   • Fewer moving parts mean less routine servicing, fewer filter changes and lower life‐cycle maintenance.

3. Increased resilience and reliability  
   • Continues to function in a power outage (as long as windows/vents can be opened)—important for emergency smoke control or keeping indoor air fresh in a blackout.  
   • Less prone to single-point failures (no central fan that can break down and shut off all ventilation).

4. Improved occupant comfort and wellbeing  
   • Many occupants report greater thermal and acoustic comfort when they can control openings (e.g. operable windows).  
   • Connection to outdoor conditions (sights, sounds) can enhance mental comfort and sense of space.  
   • High rates of fresh outdoor air can dilute indoor pollutants and support healthy indoor air quality.

5. Noise reduction  
   • Eliminates fan noise in living or working spaces; outdoor noise ingress can be managed with acoustically treated vents.

6. Lower carbon footprint  
   • By avoiding electricity-driven ventilation fans, natural ventilation cuts indirect CO₂ emissions—especially in regions where the grid is carbon-intensive.

Caveat: Natural ventilation performance depends on climate, building orientation and design (e.g. window size, placement of inlet/outlet openings) and occupant behavior. In many climates or high-performance buildings, a hybrid approach—combining natural ventilation with occasional mechanical boost—can yield the best balance of energy efficiency, indoor-air quality and user comfort.

Optimizing natural ventilation is about harnessing wind and buoyancy (stack) forces to provide fresh air, control indoor temperatures and maintain comfort without—or with minimal—mechanical systems. Here are the key strategies:

1. Building Orientation and Layout  
   • Orient the long axis of the house perpendicular to prevailing winds to maximize wind-driven airflow.  
   • Plan rooms so that “clean air” spaces (living rooms, bedrooms) face the prevailing wind, with “exhaust” spaces (kitchens, bathrooms) on the leeward side.

2. Cross-Ventilation  
   • Provide openings (windows, vents) on at least two opposite or adjacent facades.  
   • Size and position openings to create a clear, unobstructed airflow path through the occupied zones.  
   • Use operable windows of differing sizes: larger inlet windows on the windward side, smaller outlets leeward.

3. Stack Effect (Buoyancy-Driven Ventilation)  
   • Incorporate high-level openings—clerestory windows, roof vents, or ridge vents—together with low-level inlets. Warm indoor air rises and escapes through high vents, pulling cooler air in below.  
   • A “solar chimney” (a glazed shaft on the sun-facing side) will heat up and accelerate the upward flow, enhancing ventilation on calm days.

4. Window and Vent Design  
   • Use casement or louvered windows that can be angled to catch breezes and direct airflow low into the room.  
   • Install trickle vents in window frames to allow a controlled background flow even when windows are closed.  
   • Consider window-opening actuators (electric or pneumatic) tied to temperature or CO₂ sensors for automatic control.

5. Internal Airflow Paths and Zoning  
   • Keep interior doors and corridors aligned to allow free airflow between rooms.  
   • Use transfer grilles or under-door clearances to prevent “dead zones.”  
   • Zone the house so that you can isolate or open areas depending on occupancy and thermal loads.

6. Airtightness and Controlled Leakage  
   • Ironically, you need good airtightness around the building envelope to ensure that air enters and leaves only through the intended openings—not through random cracks—so you can predict and control ventilation rates.  
   • Seal around windows, doors and service penetrations; then rely on designed inlets and outlets for fresh-air supply.

7. Shading and Thermal Mass  
   • Proper shading (overhangs, shutters, vegetation) prevents solar overheating, which can reduce the temperature differential needed for effective stack ventilation.  
   • Exposed thermal mass (concrete, tile) can moderate indoor temperature swings, keeping incoming air cool.

8. Seasonal and Day/Night Strategies  
   • In summer, maximize night-time purge ventilation—open large low and high vents before dawn to flush heat stored in the structure.  
   • In shoulder seasons or mild climates, ventilate during the cooler parts of the day and close openings when outdoor temperatures rise.

9. Integration with Energy Performance  
   • In an EPC (energy performance certificate) context, natural ventilation can help reduce cooling loads and improve indoor air quality without mechanical fans, potentially improving your building’s energy class.  
   • Document your ventilation strategy and airtightness measures in the EPC so assessors understand how you balance fresh-air requirements with energy efficiency.

By carefully combining wind-driven cross-ventilation, buoyancy-driven stack effects, well-designed openings and controlled airtightness, you can achieve a high-performing natural ventilation system that keeps occupants comfortable year-round with minimal energy use.

Here are the main advantages of installing solar panels:

   • Solar panels generate electricity from sunlight, which directly offsets the amount of power you must buy from the grid.

3. Energy Independence and Security  
   • Generating your own electricity makes you less vulnerable to fluctuations in energy prices and grid outages.

   • In many countries, government incentives—such as tax credits, grants or feed-in tariffs—can significantly reduce your upfront costs.

   • Homes and commercial buildings with solar installations tend to sell faster and at higher prices, because buyers recognize the value of lower ongoing energy costs.

   • Distributed solar generation reduces peak-demand pressure on the electrical grid, improving overall stability and reducing the need for new centralized power plants.  

By converting abundant sunlight into electricity, solar panels offer both economic and environmental returns, making them a compelling investment for residential, commercial and industrial properties.

When you’re evaluating whether to invest in solar panels for a building, there are several technical, financial and regulatory factors to understand. Below is a structured checklist to help guide your decision:

1. Building and Site Assessment  
 • Roof orientation and pitch – South-facing roofs at 20–40° tilt are ideal in Sweden. East- or west-facing can work but yield is typically 10–20% lower.  
 • Shading analysis – Even small amounts of shade from trees or neighboring buildings can reduce output disproportionately. Perform a digital or on-site shade study.  
 • Structural suitability – Ensure your roof (or ground-mount structure) can safely carry the weight of panels and mounting hardware. A building inspection may be required.  
 • EPC energy class – If your building has a low energy-efficiency rating (E, F or G), you may get better returns by first improving insulation, windows or ventilation before sizing a PV system.

2. Energy Consumption and System Sizing  
 • Annual electricity use – Review your last 12 months of bills to understand your load profile. A system sized to cover 50–70% of annual use often delivers the best economic return without significant export restrictions.  
 • Peak vs. off-peak demand – If you use more power during daylight hours (e.g., manufacturing, electric heating, EV charging), you’ll self-consume a higher share of what you produce and improve your payback.

3. Technology Options  
 • Panel types – Monocrystalline panels typically offer higher efficiency (170–220 W/m²) but at a premium cost; polycrystalline are slightly less efficient but generally cheaper.  
 • Inverters – String inverters are cost-effective for uniform arrays; microinverters or power optimizers can mitigate losses from shading or differing panel orientations.  
 • Mounting systems – Roof-integrated, ballast-mounted or rail-mounted systems each have pros and cons in terms of waterproofing, cost and maintenance access.

4. Financial Analysis  
 • Upfront costs – Including panels, inverters, mounting, installation, grid-connection fees and any roof upgrades.  
 • Incentives and subsidies – Investigate national and local schemes (investment grants, tax credits, accelerated depreciation, net metering or feed-in tariffs).  
 • Payback period and ROI – Calculate based on system cost minus incentives, expected annual generation (kWh), self-consumption rate and electricity tariff. Many Swedish commercial systems aim for a 7–12 year payback.  
 • Financing options – Cash purchase, green loans, leasing or power-purchase agreements (PPAs).

5. Grid Connection and Regulations  
 • Grid-operator requirements – You’ll need approval for export capacity, a new bidirectional meter and possibly grid-upgrades.  
 • Permits and building codes – Some municipalities require building permits for roof-mounted arrays over a certain size or on heritage buildings.  
 • Fire safety and access – Compliance with rules on safe panel spacing and roof-top evacuation routes.

6. Operation, Maintenance and Monitoring  
 • Performance guarantees – Look for panel warranties of 25+ years (80–90% output guarantee) and inverter warranties of 10–15 years.  
 • Maintenance plan – Regular cleaning, inspection of wiring and monitoring for hotspots or degraded modules.  
 • Monitoring systems – Web-based portals or apps help you track real-time production, detect faults quickly and optimize performance.

7. Future-Proofing  
 • Battery storage – Adding batteries can increase self-consumption, provide backup power and support peak-shaving, but adds cost and complexity.  
 • System expansion – If you anticipate higher future demand (e.g., electric vehicle charging), design the inverter and roof layout to allow easy expansion.

By carrying out a thorough site assessment, analysing your energy needs, and running a detailed financial and regulatory review, you’ll be well equipped to decide whether a solar installation is the right investment for your building.

The building’s EPC-energy class (epc_egienergiklass) is a summary indicator of its overall yearly energy use per m².  While it doesn’t directly mandate specific white goods or electronics, it does influence how much of your total energy bill comes from appliances—and therefore how you should prioritise their efficiency.  

1. In a high-performance building (Class A–B):  
   • Heating, cooling and ventilation loads are already low, so appliances and lighting often become your single largest energy consumers.  
   • Opt for top-tier EU energy-labels (the new A–G scale or the legacy A+++/A++ labels) on refrigerators, dishwashers, laundry machines, TVs etc. This maximises the relative savings.  

2. In a low-performance building (Class E–G):  
   • Poor insulation and inefficient HVAC dominate energy use, so envelope upgrades or a new heat‐pump will usually yield larger savings than swapping out a refrigerator.  
   • That said, choosing efficient appliances is still cost-effective: they lower your overall consumption, reduce peak loads on heating and electrical circuits—and prepare you better for future building upgrades.  

3. In a mid-range building (Class C–D):  
   • You should aim for a balanced approach—combine insulation, sealing or ventilation improvements with high-efficiency appliances.  
   • A compact, well-insulated home with A- or B-rated appliances can achieve total energy savings of 20–30 % compared to the same home with mid-range equipment.  

Key takeaway: Use the EPC class to gauge where your biggest energy-saving opportunities lie. In very efficient buildings, appliances dominate the balance—so always choose the highest energy class available. In less efficient buildings, focus first on the building fabric and HVAC, but don’t overlook the cumulative impact of energy-smart appliances on your monthly bills.

When comparing refrigerators and freezers for long-term energy savings, look for the following key features:

1. High Energy-Efficiency Rating  
   • In Europe, choose appliances rated A+++ under the EU energy label (or its successor scale G–A+++).  
   • In North America, look for ENERGY STAR certification.

2. Inverter (Variable-Speed) Compressor  
   • Adapts motor speed to cooling demand rather than cycling on/off.  
   • Uses significantly less electricity, runs quieter and maintains more even temperatures.

3. Advanced Insulation  
   • Vacuum-insulated panels or expanded polyurethane foam reduce heat gain.  
   • Thicker, high-density insulation slows temperature rise when the door is opened.

4. Tight-Seal Door Gaskets  
   • Look for magnetic or silicone seals rated as “anti-microbial” or “low-leakage.”  
   • Check that doors close firmly without gaps; a good seal prevents cold air loss.

5. Automatic or Adaptive Defrosting  
   • “Frost-free” or “auto-defrost” features prevent ice buildup, so the compressor runs less frequently.  
   • Adaptive defrost algorithms only run when needed (based on door-opening frequency and humidity), saving extra energy.

6. LED Interior Lighting  
   • Consumes far less power than incandescent or halogen bulbs.  
   • Generates almost no heat, reducing the compressor’s workload.

7. Precise Digital Temperature Controls  
   • Allow you to set exact compartment temperatures (e.g., +3 °C in the fridge, –18 °C in the freezer).  
   • Some models include separate cooling zones or “super-cool”/“super-freeze” functions for rapid chilling.

8. Eco or Vacation Modes  
   • These settings lower energy use when the unit is lightly loaded or left unattended for long periods.

9. Low-GWP Refrigerant  
   • Look for models using natural refrigerants such as R600a (isobutane) or R290 (propane).  
   • They not only have a lower environmental impact but may also improve thermodynamic efficiency.

10. Size and Configuration Appropriate to Your Needs  
   • An oversized unit uses more energy even when partly empty; choose capacity to suit your household.  
   • Models with separate drawers or compartment doors let you open only one section at a time, reducing cold-air loss.

By combining a top energy-label rating with features such as an inverter compressor, high-performance insulation, smart defrost control and LED lighting, you’ll minimize electricity consumption and achieve the best long-term savings.

In Sweden (and in many other markets) you actually need two separate agreements to have electricity in your home or business:

1. Grid contract (nätavtal)  
   - Who you sign with: your local grid‐ or distribution system operator (DSO).  
   - What it covers: the physical delivery of electricity over the network to your meter.  
   - Charges involved:  
     • A fixed subscription fee (monthly or annual)  
     • A variable network fee (öre/kWh or kW)  
     • Any peak‐load or capacity charges, if applicable  
   - Why it exists: the grid operator has a regional monopoly on maintaining lines, transformers and metering equipment.  

2. Electricity supply contract (elhandelsavtal)  
   - Who you sign with: an electricity retailer (elhandelsbolag) of your choice.  
   - What it covers: the actual commodity you consume—electricity purchased on the wholesale market.  
   - Charges involved:  
     • Energy price (öre/kWh), which can be flat, indexed (spot price plus margin) or fixed over a contract term  
     • Supplier fees or service fees  
     • Any optional environmental or certification premiums (e.g. “100% renewable”)  
   - Why it exists: retailing electricity is a competitive market—customers choose supplier, product and pricing model.  

Key distinction  
– The grid contract guarantees that power can flow from the national transmission grid into your building and maintains that infrastructure.  
– The supply contract guarantees that you actually have electricity to put on the grid, and sets the per-kWh price you pay for consumption.  

Both agreements are required: without a grid contract you have no physical connection, and without a supply contract you have no energy to flow through it.

Control and regulation technology in a building‐services context refers to all the sensors, controllers, actuators and software that together monitor and adjust technical installations (heating, cooling, ventilation, lighting, etc.) so that they maintain desired set-points (temperature, airflow, humidity, indoor air quality) in the most energy-efficient and reliable way.  

Key elements and their roles:  
• Sensors – measure physical quantities such as temperature, humidity, CO₂ levels, flow rates or room occupancy.  
• Controllers/PLCs – receive sensor signals, compare them to target values (set-points) and compute how much correction is needed.  
• Actuators – valves, dampers, pumps or variable-speed drives that carry out the adjustments commanded by the controller.  
• User interfaces and software – allow facility managers or occupants to view current conditions, change set-points, schedule operating times and alarm thresholds.  
• Communication networks – fieldbuses (KNX, Modbus, BACnet, LonWorks, etc.) and IT infrastructure that link sensors, controllers, actuators and building-management systems (BMS).  

Main benefits:  
• Comfort – stable indoor climate with minimal temperature swings.  
• Energy efficiency – reduction of unnecessary heating, cooling or ventilation by running systems only as much as is needed.  
• Safety and reliability – early warning of faults or out-of-range conditions, automatic interventions (e.g. frost protection, overpressure relief).  
• Data and analytics – logging of operating data for performance optimization, preventive maintenance and compliance with energy regulations (e.g. EPC requirements).

Expanding a control system typically involves both hardware and software phases, careful planning, and rigorous testing. Below is a step-by-step overview of how you can scale or extend an existing control system—whether it’s a building‐automation system, an industrial PLC/SCADA installation or a more specialized process control network.

1. Define Requirements and Scope  
   • Identify new functions or zones to be controlled (e.g. additional HVAC zones, lighting circuits, production lines).  
   • Determine performance targets (response time, redundancy, data throughput).  
   • Establish budget, schedule and any regulatory or safety constraints.

2. Modular Hardware Expansion  
   • Add I/O Modules: Install additional digital/analog input–output cards or remote I/O racks to handle new sensors and actuators.  
   • Upgrade Controllers: If the existing PLC or DCS is at capacity, add a secondary controller or choose a higher-performance CPU module.  
   • Network Infrastructure: Expand your fieldbus or Ethernet backbone (e.g. BACnet/IP, Modbus TCP, Profinet) to reach new devices. Use managed switches or segment into VLANs if necessary.

3. Software and Configuration  
   • Program Logic Updates: Extend ladder logic, function block diagrams or structured text to incorporate the new control loops.  
   • HMI/SCADA Screens: Create or modify graphical pages to visualize and operate the new system elements.  
   • Alarm & Event Management: Define any new alarm thresholds, notifications or interlocks.

4. Integration of New Devices  
   • Sensor/Actuator Selection: Choose devices compatible with your signal types and network protocols.  
   • Communication Drivers: Install or license any required protocol drivers or gateways.  
   • Tag Mapping: Assign unique addresses or data tags for every new field device.

5. Cybersecurity and Redundancy  
   • Secure Communications: Implement firewalls, secure tunneling (VPN) and intrusion detection where remote access is needed.  
   • Redundant Topology: For critical processes, add redundant controllers or network paths to ensure failover capability.  
   • Access Control: Enforce role-based user authentication and maintain an audit trail for changes.

6. Testing and Commissioning  
   • Factory Acceptance Test (FAT): Where possible, simulate the expanded system offline to validate logic and interlocks.  
   • Site Acceptance Test (SAT): Power up and test in situ—verify I/O correctness, network latency, alarm behavior and HMI operation.  
   • Fine Tuning: Adjust PID loops, setpoints and schedules based on actual operating data.

7. Documentation and Training  
   • Update Schematics: Revise electrical and network drawings, I/O lists and control narratives.  
   • Operation Manuals: Provide step-by-step instructions for operators and maintenance staff.  
   • Training Sessions: Conduct hands-on workshops to familiarize users with new panels, software screens and procedures.

8. Ongoing Maintenance and Future Scalability  
   • Version Control: Archive backups of the expanded system configuration.  
   • Performance Monitoring: Use trend logs and analytics to detect drift or bottlenecks.  
   • Phased Upgrades: Design your architecture so further expansions can be done in plug-and-play fashion—keeping subsequent costs and downtime to a minimum.

By following a structured approach—starting with clear requirements, then layering in modular hardware, rigorous software configuration, thorough testing, and robust documentation—you’ll achieve a scalable, maintainable control system that can grow as your needs evolve.

In electric-vehicle charging terminology the line between “normal” (often called “AC charging”) and “fast” (generally “DC charging”) is normally drawn at about 22 kW:

• Normal (AC) charging  
  – Up to 3.7 kW: slow home charging  
  – 3.7 – 22 kW: faster “Mode 3” AC charging (wall boxes, public AC stations)  

• Fast (DC) charging  
  – Above 22 kW (most commonly 50 kW and up): high-power DC chargers  
  – Rapid/ultra-fast stations today can deliver 150–350 kW or more  

So in practice, any charger rated at 22 kW or below is considered “normal” AC charging, and anything above that (and especially DC-coupled equipment of 50 kW+) falls into the fast-charging category.

Load balancing in the context of EV charging is a strategy—implemented in hardware and/or software—that dynamically distributes the available electrical capacity among one or more chargers so that you never exceed the maximum draw of your electrical installation (for example, the main fuse in your home or the building’s meter cabinet). In practice this means:

1. Why it’s needed  
   • Prevents nuisance tripping of the main breaker or fuse when multiple chargers (or other heavy loads) are running simultaneously.  
   • Avoids costly upgrades to the site’s electrical infrastructure by making better use of what you already have.  
   • Helps manage peak demand on the public grid, which can reduce energy costs and grid-stabilization fees.

2. How it works  
   • Static load balancing: You set a fixed maximum total current (e.g. 32 A). The system divides that equally—or according to predefined priorities—among active charging points.  
   • Dynamic load balancing: The system continuously measures real-time power draw (from the main incoming line and/or individual chargers) and adjusts each EV’s charging current on the fly. If someone in the house turns on an oven or air-source heat pump, the EV chargers automatically back off to keep within the overall limit.  

3. Where you find it  
   • Residential wall boxes or smart home energy management systems often include basic load-balancing features.  
   • In larger installations (e.g. apartment blocks, workplaces or public charging hubs), a central controller monitors all chargers and sometimes even integrates with building-management or backend software platforms to optimize cost and grid impact.  

4. Benefits  
   • Maximizes charging speed without overloads.  
   • Provides a smoother, safer power draw profile for both the local installation and the wider electricity network.  
   • Enables “future proof” expansion—adding more chargers is often a matter of connecting new hardware rather than trenching new cables or upgrading transformers.

In Sweden, there are several ways to obtain financial support for improving the thermal insulation of apartment buildings (multi-dwelling housing). Below is an overview of the most common grants, tax deductions and subsidy programmes you can explore:

1. ROT tax deduction (“ROT-avdrag”)  
   • What it is: A tax credit of up to 30 percent (limited to a maximum amount per person and year) for labour costs when you renovate, maintain or improve your home.   
   • How it applies to insulation: Labour costs for installing or upgrading exterior wall insulation, attic insulation, basement ceiling insulation and other related work qualify for ROT. Materials are not covered by ROT, only the labour portion.  
   • Who is eligible: Owners of condominiums (bostadsrättsföreningar) can apply via the association’s contractor (the association must be VAT-registered and can pass on the ROT benefit). Individual apartment owners cannot directly claim ROT on the exterior envelope, but the association can.

2. Klimatklivet (Swedish Environmental Protection Agency)  
   • What it is: A non-repayable grant for investments that reduce greenhouse-gas emissions.  
   • How it applies to insulation: Projects improving building envelope U-values (e.g. external wall insulation, roof insulation) may be eligible.  
   • Grant level: Typically covers 30–50 percent of eligible costs, depending on project size and impact.  
   • How to apply: Applications are made online when a funding round is announced, usually twice per year. Decisions are made by the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) on behalf of the EPA.

3. Energieffektiviseringsstödet (The National Board of Housing, Building and Planning – Boverket)  
   • What it is: A targeted grant for energy-efficiency measures in existing buildings.  
   • How it applies to insulation: Multi-dwelling buildings can get 30 percent of the cost for planned improvement measures, including wall, roof and floor insulation.  
   • Special conditions: Must meet pre-defined technical requirements (e.g. maximum U-values). The project must be completed within a set timeframe (usually 2–3 years from decision date).

4. Regional and municipal energy grants  
   • What they are: Many municipalities and regional councils offer their own energy-efficiency grants, often through local energy companies or environmental offices.  
   • Scope: These can range from small “energi-checkar” for energy surveys to partial grants for upgrading façades, windows and insulation.  
   • How to find them: Check your municipality’s website under “energy and environment” or contact the municipal energy adviser (energirådgivare).

5. EU and other programmes  
   • European Structural and Investment Funds (ESIF): In some regions these funds support energy-efficiency projects in multi-dwelling buildings.  
   • Horizon Europe and demonstration grants: For innovative insulation materials or renovation methods, research and pilot projects may obtain co-funding.

Key steps to follow  
 1. Compile an energy audit (“energikartläggning”) or energy performance certificate (EPC/energideklaration) to document current U-values and pinpoint where insulation will have the greatest impact.  
 2. Compare total cost estimates with each programme’s eligibility requirements and application deadlines.  
 3. Apply formally through the relevant portal (Skatteverket for ROT, Klimatklivet via the county administrative board, Boverket’s portal for energy-efficiency grants, plus any municipal schemes).  
 4. Implement the work according to the grant decision, document invoices carefully and submit final reports to secure the subsidy disbursement.

Because rules and funding levels can change year to year, it is wise to:

Below is an overview of the most common grant and subsidy programmes in Sweden that private homeowners, housing associations and companies can apply for when investing in energy-efficiency measures. Exact terms, available funding and application windows vary over time, so always check the administrator’s website for the latest details.

1. Klimatklivet (Naturvårdsverket)  
   • Target group: Municipalities, companies, housing associations and certain organisations  
   • Eligible measures: Examples include heat-pump systems, biogas upgrades, upgraded process-heating in industry, solar parks, building envelope improvements for large buildings etc.  
   • Funding level: Typically 30–50 percent of eligible investment cost (for certain large industrial measures lower)  
   • How to apply: Online application during open call periods on Naturvårdsverket’s website  

2. Investeringsstöd för flerbostadshus (Boverket)  
   • Target group: Housing associations and private landlords with multi-dwelling buildings  
   • Eligible measures: Façade insulation, replacement of windows/doors, installation of energy-efficient ventilation, heat pumps, solar cells, LED lighting in common areas etc.  
   • Funding level: Up to 30 percent of investment cost (higher levels possible for heritage buildings)  
   • How to apply: Via Boverket’s portal when the call is open (generally two calls per year)  

3. Stöd för solceller (Energimyndigheten)  
   • Target group: Private homeowners, associations, companies, public sector  
   • Eligible measures: Purchase and installation of solar-PV systems on rooftops or ground-mounted  
   • Funding level: Flat amount per installed kW (e.g. SEK 1 200–1 600 per kW) with a maximum grant per installation  
   • How to apply: Online application on Energimyndigheten’s website  

4. ROT-avdrag for Energy Measures (Skatteverket)  
   • Target group: Private individuals  
   • Eligible measures: Labor costs for insulation work, new energy-efficient windows, installation of heat pumps, ventilation improvements, solar-PV installation, etc.  
   • Deduction level: 30 percent of eligible labor cost, up to SEK 50 000 per person and year  
   • How to apply: Handled via your contractor, who deducts the subsidy directly on your invoice  

5. Länsstyrelsernas regionala stöd  
   • Target group: Often private homeowners and small businesses  
   • Eligible measures: Varies by county (ex. barn conversion to energy-efficient housing, pilot projects, local energy-saving campaigns)  
   • Funding level: Depends on regional budget and programme  
   • How to apply: Contact your county administrative board (Länsstyrelsen) or check their website for current calls  

6. EU-finansiering (ex. LIFE, ELENA, Horizon Europe)  
   • Target group: Large public-private partnerships, municipalities, research institutions, industry consortia  
   • Eligible measures: Large-scale or innovative pilot projects in energy efficiency, smart grids, building renovation, district heating, etc.  
   • Funding level: Varies by programme (often 40–85 percent)  
   • How to apply: Through EU’s Funding & Tenders Portal  

7. Banker och Energikartläggningscheckar  
   • Vissa banker erbjuder “gröna lån” eller tysta ränterabatter för certifierade energieffektiviseringar.  
   • Energikartläggningscheckar (Energimyndigheten) can subsidise up to 50 percent of the cost of a professional energy audit for companies.  

Key steps before applying  
1. Inventory and energy audit – document current energy use and potential measures.  
2. Check eligibility criteria and open calls – each programme has specific technical and administrative requirements.  
3. Prepare quotations and technical specifications – most grants require at least two competitive bids.  
4. Submit application before the deadline – ensure all supporting documents are attached.  
5. Implement measure and report – most grants require reporting of final costs, energy savings and, in some cases, third-party verification.  

Always start by visiting the administrator’s website (Naturvårdsverket, Boverket, Energimyndigheten or your Länsstyrelse) to download the current guidelines, technical annexes and application forms.

Improving lighting in basement areas involves a combination of enhanced natural‐light strategies, appropriate fixture selection, thoughtful layout and smart controls. Below are several approaches:

1. Increase Natural Light  
• Install light wells or window wells. By excavating around existing basement windows and lining the wells with reflective material, you allow more daylight to penetrate.  
• Use sun tunnels (tube skylights). These capture daylight on the roof and pipe it down into interior spaces with minimal heat loss.  
• Maximize window size and glazing quality. Where code permits, enlarge below-grade windows or replace single‐glass units with high-performance double-glazed windows.

2. Select Appropriate Fixtures  
• LED fixtures. Choose high‐efficacy LED panels, troffers or downlights with a color temperature of 3000 – 4000 K for a neutral, daylight-balanced appearance.  
• High‐bay or canopy luminaires. In higher‐ceiling areas (e.g., utility or storage rooms), use LED high‐bays for uniform illumination.  
• Wall-mounted sconces or uplights. These can wash walls and ceilings with light, reducing glare and shadows.

3. Optimize Light Distribution  
• Layer ambient, task and accent lighting. Provide a base layer of general illumination (ambient), supplemented by task lights at workstations or desks and accent lights to highlight architectural features or artwork.  
• Use reflectance‐boosting finishes. Paint walls and ceilings in light, matte colors (e.g., soft white or pastel tones) to improve light diffusion and minimize glare.  
• Position fixtures to avoid deep shadows. Arrange linear fixtures along the perimeter and center to fill corners and under-window areas.

4. Incorporate Controls and Sensors  
• Dimming controls. Allow users to adjust light levels according to activity, enhancing comfort and saving energy.  
• Occupancy or vacancy sensors. In infrequently used spaces (storage, laundry, mechanical rooms), sensors ensure lights operate only when the space is occupied.  
• Daylight-harvesting controls. In areas served by sun tunnels or windows, dim electric lighting when sufficient daylight is present.

5. Address Safety and Code Requirements  
• Emergency and exit lighting. Install battery-backed emergency luminaires and illuminated exit signs in accordance with local fire and building codes.  
• Minimum illuminance levels. Target general areas at least 100–200 lux, and task areas (workbenches, laundry counters) at 300–500 lux, per recommendations in EN 12464-1 or local standards.

6. Maintenance and Upkeep  
• Keep fixtures and lenses clean. Dust and dirt can reduce output by up to 30 %.  
• Replace aging lamps promptly. Even LEDs lose lumen output over time; follow manufacturer’s recommended replacement intervals.  

By combining enhanced daylight access, high‐efficiency fixtures, layered illumination and smart controls, you can transform a dim basement into a bright, welcoming, and energy-efficient space.

Always check your local building code or property-management guidelines, since some municipalities or landlords may require a higher minimum.

Improving your building’s energy efficiency typically involves measures in three main areas: the thermal envelope, the technical systems, and user behavior/controls. Here’s how you can prioritize:  

1. Carry Out an Energy Audit  
   • Before investing in upgrades, commission a qualified energy auditor or use an accredited energy performance certificate (EPC) assessor to identify your building’s biggest losses.  
   • The audit will quantify heat losses through walls, roofs, windows and doors, as well as inefficiencies in heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting systems.  

2. Upgrade the Thermal Envelope  
   • Insulation: Add, replace or top up insulation in lofts, pitched roofs, flat roofs and cavity walls. Improving U-values reduces heat loss and lowers heating demand.  
   • Air-tightness: Seal gaps around windows, doors, service penetrations and at junctions between construction elements. An air-tight building requires less energy to heat and keeps drafts—and drafts-related heat loss—at bay.  
   • Windows and doors: Consider high-performance triple- or double-glazed units with low-emissivity coatings and thermally broken frames.  

3. Optimize Heating, Cooling and Ventilation  
   • Heating system: Replace old boilers with high-efficiency condensing boilers, air- or ground-source heat pumps, or hybrid solutions sized to your building’s reduced heat demand.  
   • Ventilation with heat recovery: Install a balanced mechanical ventilation system (MVHR) that recovers up to 90 % of the heat from exhaust air, while supplying fresh filtered air.  
   • Controls and zoning: Upgrade to smart thermostats, weather-compensated controls and radiator or floor-heating thermostatic valves. Zoning allows you to heat only occupied areas.  

4. Improve Domestic Hot Water and Appliances  
   • Water-heater efficiency: Replace electric or old gas water heaters with on-demand (tankless) systems or heat-pump water heaters.  
   • Low-flow fixtures: Fit low-flow taps, showerheads and dual-flush toilets to reduce hot-water consumption.  
   • Efficient appliances: Choose A +++ rated white goods and encourage occupants to use energy-saving settings.  

5. Upgrade Lighting and Electrical Systems  
   • LED lighting: Replace incandescent or fluorescent lamps with LEDs, which use up to 80 % less electricity and last significantly longer.  
   • Daylight harvesting and occupancy sensors: Automate lighting so it dims or switches off when natural light is sufficient or rooms are unoccupied.  

6. Integrate Renewable Energy Sources  
   • Solar photovoltaics (PV): Install PV panels on suitable roof surfaces to generate electricity on-site and reduce grid imports.  
   • Solar thermal: Use roof-mounted solar collectors to pre-heat domestic hot water.  
   • Small-scale wind or ground-based micro-generation (where locally viable).  

7. Implement Energy Monitoring and Maintenance  
   • Sub-metering: Install energy meters on major systems (heating, cooling, lighting) to track usage and pinpoint irregularities.  
   • Building management system (BMS): Use automated controls for HVAC, lighting and shading to optimize performance.  
   • Regular commissioning and maintenance: Keep systems clean, well-tuned and operating at their design efficiency.  

8. Engage Occupants  
   • Training and awareness: Educate occupants on energy-saving practices—appropriate thermostat settings, responsible use of windows and vents, turning off equipment.  
   • Feedback tools: Provide visible dashboards or apps showing real-time energy use to encourage conservation.  

By systematically addressing these areas—starting with an energy audit to set priorities—you can target the measures that will deliver the biggest energy-and-cost savings and move your building to a higher EPC energy class.

Ventilation balancing is the process of adjusting and commissioning a building’s mechanical ventilation system so that the actual airflows (supply and exhaust) in each room or zone match the design intentions. Proper balancing ensures that:

• Airflow targets are met everywhere  
  – Each room receives the correct volume of fresh air and exhaust air, avoiding over- or under-ventilation.  
• Pressure differences are controlled  
  – Balanced supply and exhaust flows minimize unintended infiltration (air leaking in through cracks) or exfiltration (air leaking out), both of which can carry heat in or out of the building.  
• Heat-recovery units operate optimally  
  – In systems with heat exchangers, balanced airflow maximizes heat (or cooling) recovery from the exhaust stream back into the incoming fresh air.  

Impact on energy use  
1. Reduced heating and cooling losses  
   If a ventilation system is unbalanced, you may be bringing in more cold air in winter (or warm air in summer) than intended, forcing the heating or cooling system to work harder. Proper balancing keeps fresh-air rates at design levels and lets heat-recovery equipment achieve its specified efficiency (often 60–90 %).  
2. Lower fan energy consumption  
   Fans draw more power when they operate against higher pressure differentials or oversized flow rates. By adjusting dampers, fan speeds or variable-air-volume (VAV) controls to the required setpoints, you avoid wasted fan power.  
3. Improved overall HVAC performance  
   When ventilation is in balance, the HVAC system as a whole runs more smoothly: temperature and humidity control is steadier, equipment cycles less frequently, and maintenance needs tend to decrease.  

In practice, ventilation balancing is carried out during commissioning by measuring airflow with calibrated instruments (anemometers, pitot tubes or flow hoods), then fine-tuning dampers, valves and fan speeds. The result is healthier indoor air quality, greater comfort and meaningful energy savings over the life of the building.

Yes. Turning down your indoor thermostat is one of the simplest and most effective ways to cut heating energy use. Here’s why and how much you can typically save:

1. Energy savings per °C  
   • Every degree you lower the set-point (for example from 21 °C to 20 °C) reduces your heating demand by roughly 5 %–7 %.  
   • If you normally heat 1 000 kWh per year, a 1 °C setback could save about 50–70 kWh annually.

2. Cost savings  
   • Those kWh savings directly translate into lower energy bills. At a unit cost of 1 kr/kWh, reducing use by 70 kWh saves about 70 kr per °C each heating season.  
   • Over several degrees, or with multiple occupants/apartments, the cumulative savings can be substantial.

3. Comfort strategies  
   • Night setbacks: Lower the temperature by 3–4 °C while you sleep or when the home is unoccupied. Modern thermostats make it easy to schedule these setbacks automatically.  
   • Zone heating: If you have thermostatic radiator valves or zoned controls, reduce temperature in rooms you seldom use.  
   • Insulation and air-tightness: The better insulated and sealed your building, the longer it retains heat, and the more effective each degree of setback becomes.

4. Health and indoor climate  
   • The Swedish National Board of Health and Welfare recommends bedroom temperatures of 16–18 °C for restful sleep and living areas around 20–21 °C.  
   • Wearing a light sweater or using extra blankets in cooler rooms helps you stay comfortable even at lower set-points.

5. Environmental impact  
   • Lowering your heating demand reduces fuel combustion (whether electricity, gas or district heat), cutting your CO₂ emissions proportionally.  
   • It’s a no-cost measure that complements investments in insulation, windows or more efficient heating systems.

In short, each degree you dial back your thermostat is a low-hanging fruit in your energy-saving toolbox. Even modest setbacks—especially overnight and when you’re out—add up to meaningful reductions in both costs and carbon footprint.

1. Building envelope improvements  
   • Loft/roof insulation – often under-insulated in older buildings.  
   • External wall insulation or cavity-wall fill – reduces heat losses through the façade.  
   • Basement/floor insulation – limits ground-borne heat leakage.  
   • Window and door upgrades – install energy-efficient glazing (e.g. low-E), proper sealing and weather-stripping.

2. Ventilation with heat recovery  
   • Mechanical supply and exhaust ventilation with high-efficiency heat recoverers (HRV/ERV units) can recapture up to 80 % of the heat in the outgoing air.  
   • Ensure ductwork is well sealed and balanced.  

3. Heating system optimization  
   • If on district heating (common in Stockholm), optimize flow temperatures and control systems (weather-compensated or room-by-room thermostats).  
   • Where oil or electric boilers remain, consider replacing with a ground- or air-source heat pump.  
   • Add smart controls and building automation (e.g. BMS) for dynamic scheduling and demand-response.  

4. Renewable generation and on-site production  
   • Solar photovoltaic panels on south-facing roofs or façades to offset common-area electricity.  
   • Solar thermal for domestic hot water support.  

5. Lighting and small-power loads  
   • Replace remaining fluorescent or halogen fixtures with LED luminaires and occupancy-daylight sensors in corridors, stairwells and communal spaces.  
   • Encourage tenants to switch to energy-efficient appliances and implement submeters where feasible.

 3. Prioritize measures by cost-effectiveness and payback time, starting with envelope sealing and insulation, then ventilation heat-recovery and heating-system controls.
